title: Microsoft Releases Aspire 13.5 With a Refreshed Dashboard and Workflow Improvements
gist: Microsoft's Aspire 13.5 shifts from the prior releases' language/deployment-target expansion to dashboard polish and quality-of-life work, bringing TypeScript AppHosts to general availability, adding Kubernetes persistent-volume modeling and cross-scope Azure resource references, broadening CLI distribution, and — notably — removing the dashboard's AI Assistant chat feature.

insights.claim: Aspire 13.5 marks an explicit pivot from the feature-expansion focus of earlier 13.x releases (new languages, deployment targets, coding-agent support) to dashboard polish and quality-of-life work, with Microsoft stating it checked contrast and accessibility across the refreshed UI while keeping layout and feature locations unchanged.
insights.speaker: Almir Vuk
insights.so_what: Signals a maturing product cycle moving from breadth to refinement, useful context for teams timing an Aspire adoption or upgrade around stability versus new capability.
insights.locator: The most immediate change is visual

insights.claim: Aspire's Interaction Service gained file-import support: a resource command can now open a file picker for JSON or YAML with a size limit and receive the contents as a stream directly, replacing the previous workaround of placing a file in a preset directory before running a script.
insights.speaker: Almir Vuk
insights.so_what: Removes a specific integration-authoring friction point for teams building custom setup or import flows on top of Aspire.
insights.locator: The Interaction Service, which lets a resource command ask for input

insights.claim: Aspire 13.5 adds an experimental in-dashboard terminal via WithTerminal(), giving a resource an interactive terminal session for shells and REPLs, letting users switch between replicas and supporting multiple simultaneous viewers attached to the same process.
insights.speaker: Almir Vuk
insights.so_what: An experimental feature worth monitoring before relying on it in production tooling workflows, but signals Aspire absorbing more of the local dev debugging loop into its dashboard.
insights.locator: Aspire 13.5 also puts a terminal inside the dashboard

insights.claim: TypeScript AppHosts reached general availability in Aspire 13.5, closing feature parity with C# (Interaction Service, file uploads, progress dialogs, custom health checks, container file copying) and removing the prior experimental opt-in requirement.
insights.speaker: Almir Vuk
insights.so_what: Lowers adoption risk for teams that want to standardize Aspire orchestration on TypeScript rather than C#, now that it is a fully supported, non-experimental path.
insights.locator: Another notable change is that TypeScript AppHosts are now generally available

insights.claim: New persistent-volume modeling lets Aspire applications configure Kubernetes storage class, capacity, and access mode before binding a volume to a project or container, with Aspire automatically emitting the PersistentVolumeClaim and rendering the workload accordingly.
insights.speaker: Almir Vuk
insights.so_what: Reduces manual Kubernetes YAML authoring for stateful workloads deployed through Aspire, relevant to teams evaluating Aspire as a Kubernetes deployment abstraction layer.
insights.locator: On deployment, the update lets applications model persistent volumes

insights.claim: New methods let an Aspire application reference existing Azure resources across resource groups, subscriptions, and tenants while keeping environment-specific details out of the AppHost source code, separating deployment intent from environment configuration.
insights.speaker: Almir Vuk
insights.so_what: Relevant to enterprises with multi-subscription or multi-tenant Azure estates that want environment-agnostic application definitions rather than hardcoded resource references.
insights.locator: New methods also let an application reference existing Azure resources

insights.claim: The Aspire CLI can now be installed and updated through mainstream package managers — Homebrew, WinGet, npm, Nix, mise, and NuGet — broadening its distribution beyond a bespoke installer.
insights.speaker: Almir Vuk
insights.so_what: Lowers the operational friction of adopting and keeping the Aspire CLI current across heterogeneous developer environments.
insights.locator: the Aspire command-line interface can now be installed and updated

insights.claim: The Aspire Visual Studio Code extension was rebranded and gained a dashboard side panel, Bun and MAUI debugging support, and resource commands surfaced directly in the tree view, deepening in-editor integration.
insights.speaker: Almir Vuk
insights.so_what: Expands Aspire's addressable workflows to Bun and MAUI developers who previously had weaker in-editor support.
insights.locator: The Visual Studio Code extension was also rebranded

themes.theme: Breaking changes, including a walked-back AI feature

insights.claim: Aspire 13.5's breaking changes include renaming the ServiceProvider property to Services, deprecating the GitHub Models integration, and removing the dashboard's AI Assistant chat feature entirely — notable because it walks back a previously shipped AI-chat capability rather than expanding it.
insights.speaker: Almir Vuk
insights.so_what: Worth watching whether this is an isolated feature cut or signals Microsoft deprioritizing embedded AI chat inside developer-tooling dashboards in favor of external agent/Copilot integrations.
insights.locator: The release further carries a number of breaking changes
